title: The Theory of Two Truths in Tibet

summaries.example: Imagine a sprout growing from a seed. We can see its color and shape, and we can talk about how it grows. Gelug thinkers say the sprout also has an empty nature: it does not exist all by itself, apart from causes and conditions. Other Tibetan thinkers emphasize that ordinary people and awakened people understand the sprout in very different ways.
summaries.summary: The entry explains how Tibetan Buddhist philosophers discuss the theory of two truths. Conventional truth concerns the ordinary world of appearances, names, and practical experiences. Ultimate truth concerns reality as understood by awakened wisdom. The four major Tibetan traditions discussed here—Nyingma, Kagyü, Sakya, and Gelug—share a connection with the Prāsaṅgika form of Madhyamaka and respect Candrakīrti as an important interpreter of Nāgārjuna. They nevertheless disagree about what is divided into the two truths, whether the difference belongs to objects or to minds, and how the two truths are related. Nyingma, Kagyü, and Sakya mainly explain the division through contrasting ways of knowing: confused ordinary cognition and nonconfused wisdom. Gelug instead argues that each conventionally existing thing has both a conventional nature and an ultimate nature. The entry studies these philosophical disagreements rather than giving a simple history of the schools.
key_ideas: Tibetan philosophers call conventional truth and ultimate truth the “two truths.”
The Nyingma, Kagyü, Sakya, and Gelug schools all follow the Prāsaṅgika approach, but they explain the two truths differently.
A major question is whether the two truths belong to things themselves or to different ways of understanding things.
Nyingma, Kagyü, and Sakya stress the difference between confused ordinary understanding and awakened wisdom. Gelug says one thing can have both a conventional nature and an ultimate nature.
The theory is connected with understanding reality and with the Buddhist goal of freedom from suffering.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic shows that people within one broad religious and philosophical tradition can agree on a central question while giving careful, different answers. It also asks how appearances, language, reasoning, and wisdom are connected. Studying the debate can help us notice the difference between what seems true at first and what careful investigation may reveal.

important_terms.definition: A Buddhist idea that things do not have a completely independent, unchanging essence of their own.
The everyday level of appearances, names, and experiences. Different Tibetan schools explain its status in different ways.
The deepest reality, understood through wisdom rather than ordinary confused thinking.
A Tibetan Buddhist philosophical approach that uses reasoning to challenge fixed ideas instead of defending one permanent theory.
A Buddhist school of thought connected with the Middle Way. The Tibetan schools in this entry all identify with its approach.

questions_to_think_about: Can something look real in everyday life but be understood differently after careful investigation?
Are two different ways of seeing one thing enough to call them two truths?
Why might a philosopher say that an object depends on causes and conditions?
What could be helpful about comparing ordinary understanding with awakened wisdom?

summaries.example: Consider a table. In ordinary experience it has a shape, color, and practical function, and people can refer to it by a shared name. A Gelug analysis says the table’s conventional nature and its emptiness are aspects of one entity: the table is dependently arisen and therefore lacks an independent essence. Nyingma, Kagyü, and Sakya approaches place more emphasis on the contrasting cognitive perspectives through which conventionality and ultimacy are disclosed. The example illustrates why the debate is not merely about whether a table exists, but about what counts as the basis, definition, and relation of the two truths.
summaries.summary: The entry examines the Tibetan debate over the two truths within four traditions: Nyingma, Kagyü, Sakya, and Gelug. The shared framework is Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka, interpreted through the authority of Candrakīrti, but agreement at that level does not eliminate major disagreements. The debate concerns the basis of the distinction, the definitions of conventional and ultimate truth, the number and kinds of conventional truths, and whether the truths are identical, distinct, or related in some other way. Nyingma, Kagyü, and Sakya tend to make cognition or perspective central. They describe conventionality through the confused, deceptive cognition of ordinary beings and ultimacy through wisdom that is free from such confusion, though their accounts differ in emphasis. Kagyü is especially concerned to separate definitions from illustrative cases and often refuses to characterize the truths as simply identical or separate. Sakya presents conventional truth as ignorance-dependent appearance and ultimate truth as transcendent wisdom. Gelug takes objects of knowledge as the basis and develops a two-nature theory: each conventionally real phenomenon has a deceptive conventional mode and a nondeceptive ultimate mode. These modes are conceptually distinct but belong to one entity. Gelug connects this unity with dependent arising and emptiness, arguing that emptiness must not be confused with sheer nonexistence. The debate therefore concerns not only metaphysical structure but also standards of knowledge and the path to liberation.
key_ideas: The entry treats the two-truths theory as central not only to ontology, or the study of what exists, but also to epistemology, the study of knowing, and soteriology, the study of liberation.

Tibetan Prāsaṅgika philosophers agree on Candrakīrti’s importance but debate whether Prāsaṅgika has a positive philosophical position of its own, how the two truths are defined, and what serves as their basis.

Nyingma generally presents conventional truth as deceptive appearance for ordinary cognition and ultimate truth as reality disclosed by nondeceptive awakened cognition; it also discusses both epistemic and analytic formulations.

Kagyü distinguishes a definition from the examples used to illustrate it and often presents the two truths as neither identical nor separate. It gives the Prāsaṅgika project a strongly corrective and pedagogical role.

Sakya treats the division primarily in terms of cognition: ignorance presents conventional appearances, while wisdom in meditative equipoise realizes ultimacy. It therefore gives the two truths a sharper separation.

Gelug argues that objects of knowledge are the basis of division. Its two-nature theory holds that a single conventionally real phenomenon has both a conventional and an ultimate nature, which are one entity but conceptually distinct.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate matters because it links three philosophical questions: what phenomena are like, how they are known, and how insight changes a person’s relation to suffering. It also demonstrates that “two truths” is not a single formula with one universally accepted interpretation in Tibet. Comparing the schools helps clarify the consequences of choosing an object-based, cognition-based, or relational account of philosophical distinctions. In particular, the Gelug and non-Gelug positions show how different theories of the relation between appearance and emptiness can shape views about knowledge, practice, and awakening.

important_terms.definition: The view that phenomena arise through dependence on causes, conditions, parts, and conceptual or linguistic relations rather than existing independently.
A cognition or object that is not misleading with respect to the way things are.
A cognition that takes phenomena to possess a reality they do not have; in the entry, ordinary cognition is often described this way.
The basis or ground from which the two truths are distinguished. Tibetan schools disagree about whether this is objects, minds, or cognitive perspectives.
The claim that one phenomenon has a conventional nature and an ultimate nature, which supports Gelug’s account of the two truths.
A Middle Way philosophical approach associated in this entry with Candrakīrti, emphasizing critique of fixed philosophical positions.
The reality or mode of existence of a phenomenon when analyzed as lacking intrinsic, independent existence.
The practical Buddhist concern with liberation from suffering and the path or knowledge that supports it.

questions_to_think_about: If conventional phenomena are deceptive in one sense, in what sense can they still support ordinary knowledge and action?
Does saying that two truths are “one entity but different conceptual identities” avoid the alternatives of complete identity and complete separation?
Why does Gelug connect emptiness with dependent arising rather than with nonexistence?
What changes when the basis of the distinction is taken to be cognition rather than an object?
Can a philosophical critique be useful without committing itself to a positive theory?

summaries.example: Suppose a student sees a shadow and thinks it is a person. The shadow appears real to the student, but a closer look corrects the mistake. This is only an analogy, not a complete explanation of Buddhist philosophy. It helps show why several Tibetan schools connect conventional truth with confused or mistaken understanding, while ultimate truth is linked with a clearer, nondeceptive way of knowing. Gelug adds a different point: one thing can be discussed both as an everyday object and in terms of its emptiness, without treating those as two separate objects.
summaries.summary: This entry studies a major philosophical debate in Tibetan Buddhism: how to understand the two truths. Conventional truth concerns ordinary appearances, language, and practical experience. Ultimate truth concerns reality as understood through a nondeceptive form of wisdom. Nyingma, Kagyü, Sakya, and Gelug all identify with Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka and give Candrakīrti a central interpretive role, but they do not offer the same account. Nyingma explains the truths through the contrast between deceptive ordinary cognition and awakened cognition, while also discussing whether what is ultimate can withstand careful reasoning. Kagyü emphasizes that philosophers should not confuse a definition with the examples used to explain it. It often says that the truths are neither simply identical nor simply separate. Sakya likewise makes different cognitive perspectives central, presenting conventionality as linked with ignorance and ultimacy with wisdom. Gelug takes objects of knowledge as the basis for the distinction. According to its two-nature theory, a single phenomenon has both a conventional nature and an ultimate nature: these are not two separate things, but they are understood through different conceptual approaches. Gelug connects the ultimate nature with emptiness and the conventional nature with dependent arising and ordinary functioning. The disagreement is therefore about metaphysics, knowledge, and the path toward liberation, not merely about vocabulary.
key_ideas: The four Tibetan traditions discussed—Nyingma, Kagyü, Sakya, and Gelug—share a Prāsaṅgika identity but disagree about how to explain its implications.
The central contrast is between conventional truth, connected with ordinary appearances and confused cognition, and ultimate truth, connected with nondeceptive wisdom.
Nyingma, Kagyü, and Sakya generally make the knowing mind or perspective central to the division between the truths.
Gelug says that objects of knowledge are the basis of division and that each conventionally real thing has both a conventional and an ultimate nature.

The schools also disagree about the relationship between the truths: some stress their dependence on different perspectives, while Gelug describes them as one entity with different conceptual identities.
These ideas are tied to Buddhist practice because understanding reality is connected with overcoming confusion and reaching liberation.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic matters because it asks how appearances can be useful without being completely reliable. It also shows how different answers to one question can affect views about reasoning, meditation, ordinary experience, and liberation. Reading the debate carefully encourages intellectual humility: philosophers may share important commitments while still disagreeing about whether truth is divided by objects, minds, or ways of knowing.

important_terms.definition: The everyday truth of things as they appear, are named, and are used in ordinary life, even though that appearance may be misleading in deeper analysis.
The truth understood through a nondeceptive and deeply informed way of knowing, often connected with awakened wisdom.
A mistaken way of understanding that treats things as more independent or solid than they really are.
The Buddhist idea that things arise through causes and conditions and do not stand alone by themselves.
A philosophical term for what something is like in itself or what makes it the kind of thing it is.
A way of reasoning associated with Candrakīrti that challenges an opponent’s assumptions and does not simply set up a fixed system of its own.
A Tibetan Buddhist tradition that, in this debate, explains the two truths through one object’s conventional and ultimate natures.
A Tibetan Buddhist tradition whose thinkers emphasize that the two truths are distinguished through contrasting kinds of cognition or perspective.

questions_to_think_about: If two people understand the same object differently, does that create two truths or two viewpoints?
Why might a school distinguish a thing’s everyday nature from its deeper nature?
How can emptiness avoid meaning that nothing exists at all?
What might be gained by criticizing an opponent’s assumptions instead of defending a complete theory?
Why would a theory of truth matter for a person’s spiritual practice?
